children: Treasury secretaries have traditionally been masters of cautious policy speak. Scott Bessent is letting his hedge-fund roots show.
Speaking yesterday at Southern Methodist University, the former macro trader was remarkably candid about the role he sees himself playing in the market.
"Whenever people say, 'Oh, well, Treasury Secretary's taking a risk,' well, you know, it's my dream," he said. "I have asymmetric information. I am the house now."

"When we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Japanese, what the Bank of Japan's going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do," Bessent continued. "You can bet against me if you want."

Bessent's comments-made during lengthy remarks also touching on higher education and AI-come just weeks after Washington conducted a rare joint intervention with Tokyo to prop up the yen. He has since been criticized for intervening in markets, including with the surprise announcement that the Treasury would step up buybacks of long-term debt to curb borrowing costs.

The results have been mixed: Treasury yields continue to push higher, including today. Meanwhile, the yen initially weakened in the days following the joint intervention-but it has recently been climbing.

Before joining the Trump administration last year, Bessent had a long career as a hedge-fund manager. He was one of the driving forces behind George Soros's firm's enormous bet that the British pound would collapse in the early 1990s-a wager that netted the firm more than $1 billion.
Years later, he scored another massive win shorting the Japanese yen-the very currency he's now trying to prop up.
